89.title: One goal, as in Lens
89.standfirst: In 1998 France needed the World Cup's first golden goal to get past Paraguay. Twenty-eight years later, in Philadelphia heat, they needed a penalty — and little else changed.
prose: On the evening of the Fourth of July, in heat that slowed everything except the clock, France beat Paraguay 1-0 at Lincoln Financial Field. Kylian Mbappé converted a 70th-minute penalty — his 19th World Cup goal — and Les Bleus moved into a fourth consecutive quarter-final. For Paraguay, a first World Cup in sixteen years ended in the round of 16. For France, a tournament that had been all fluency finally asked for patience instead, and got it.

France and Paraguay had met at a World Cup only twice before, and both meetings sit oddly in the memory. In Sweden in 1958, France won 7-3, Just Fontaine scoring a hat-trick on the way to his thirteen goals, a record still unbroken. Forty years later, in Lens, the sides played 113 scoreless minutes — Zinedine Zidane suspended, José Luis Chilavert repelling everything — until Laurent Blanc turned in David Trezeguet's header in the 114th, the first golden goal ever scored at a World Cup. France went on to win that tournament. Didier Deschamps captained that side; on Saturday he watched from the touchline as the pattern repeated at a gentler tempo.

Paraguay had waited a long time for this stage. Absent since the 2010 quarter-final in South Africa, where eventual champions Spain edged them out, Gustavo Alfaro's side opened this tournament with a 1-4 defeat to the United States and then conceded twice in four matches. They beat Türkiye 1-0, drew with Australia, and in Boston held Germany to 1-1 before winning the shoot-out 4-3 — the first penalty shoot-out Germany have ever lost at a World Cup. Their goals came sparingly all summer: three in five matches, one each from Mauricio, Matías Galarza and Julio Enciso.

France have scored fourteen times in five games — 3-1 against Senegal, 3-0 against Iraq on this same Philadelphia pitch, 4-1 against Norway, 3-0 against Sweden, and now the one here — with the goals concentrated where you would expect: seven for Mbappé, four for Ousmane Dembélé, two for Bradley Barcola, one for Désiré Doué. Paraguay gave that attack its quietest night of the month. Gómez's back line sat deep, the heat did the rest, and for seventy minutes the game had the shape of Lens. Then came the penalty, and Mbappé, and a lead Paraguay had not scored enough all tournament to threaten.

So the tie closed two ledgers at once. Paraguay went home with the Germany shoot-out as the keepsake of a return sixteen years in the making, the 2010 quarter-final still their high-water mark. France moved on to a quarter-final of their own, a fourth in succession, every one of them reached under Deschamps — who said eighteen months ago that this tournament would be his last. The scoreline against Paraguay remains what it was in 1998: one goal, eventually, and no way back.
threads: Laurent Blanc's 114th-minute winner in Lens in 1998 was the first golden goal in World Cup history.
Mbappé's penalty was his 19th World Cup goal and his seventh of this tournament.
France have won all three World Cup meetings: 7-3 in 1958, 1-0 in 1998, 1-0 in 2026.
This was France's fourth consecutive quarter-final, all four under Deschamps, in his final tournament in charge.
89.meaning: Paraguay rebuilt the wall of Lens; France, once again, needed only one way through.

90.title: Same opponent, wider gap
90.standfirst: Morocco's 3-0 win in Houston ended the best World Cup a Canadian men's team has played and set up a quarter-final against France, a rematch of the 2022 semi-final. The only previous meeting between the two ended the same way: Morocco advancing, Canada going home.
prose: The co-hosts' World Cup ended at midday in Houston, a long way from home in more than one sense. Morocco's 3-0 win at NRG Stadium carried them into a second consecutive quarter-final and closed the deepest run a Canadian men's side has ever made. It also confirmed the cost of the Switzerland defeat in the final group game, which took away top spot and any knockout football on home soil; a tournament Canada part-owns finished, for them, in Los Angeles and then Texas.

These teams had met once before at a World Cup, and that afternoon decided things too. In Doha in December 2022, Hakim Ziyech capitalised on a defensive mistake inside four minutes, Youssef En-Nesyri added a second, and Nayef Aguerd's own goal gave Canada only consolation in a 2-1 defeat that sent Morocco through as group winners — their first knockout place in 36 years — and sent Canada home without a point. Morocco went on to a first African semi-final and fourth place. The distance between the two programmes has not narrowed since.

Morocco arrived in Houston unbeaten in this tournament, as they have been almost everywhere lately — BBC Sport put their run at 34 matches without defeat. They had drawn with Brazil, beaten Scotland and Haiti, and then held their nerve in Monterrey to put out the Netherlands on penalties. Canada's group stage contained the men's programme's first World Cup point and first win, a 6-0 dismantling of Qatar, and the 1-0 round-of-32 result against South Africa was a first knockout victory. Alphonso Davies, who tore an ACL on international duty in March 2025, was never fully himself here; the Guardian has since reported that the exit revived questions over how his recovery was managed.

For half the match Canada stayed in it. On 50 minutes Azzedine Ounahi put Morocco ahead, and the game found its level. Morocco's goals had been shared around this summer — Ismael Saibari with three, Achraf Hakimi and Soufiane Rahimi among the others — and here the load passed to Ounahi, the Girona midfielder who first announced himself at Qatar 2022. His second came on 82 minutes, his first two goals of the tournament arriving in a single afternoon, with Rahimi scoring the other. Jonathan David, Canada's leading scorer with three, was given nothing by the back line protecting Yassine Bounou, and Morocco recorded a second clean sheet of the tournament.

What the win opened for Morocco is the fixture the bracket had been holding back: France in Boston on 9 July, a rematch of the 2022 semi-final that France won 2-0. Across this World Cup and the last, Morocco have removed Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Canada from World Cup knockout rounds, and the question of whether they belong among the tournament's heaviest names is no longer seriously asked. For Canada, the accounting is quieter: a first point, a first win, a first knockout victory — and a hard reading of what the Davies episode cost, before Jesse Marsch's side decide what comes next.
threads: Azzedine Ounahi's goals on 50 and 82 minutes were his first two of the tournament.
Across 2022 and 2026, Morocco have removed Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Canada from World Cup knockout rounds.
Canada's first men's World Cup point, first win and first knockout victory all came at this tournament.
Morocco's quarter-final against France in Boston on 9 July is a rematch of the 2022 semi-final.
90.meaning: Canada found out how far they have come; Morocco showed them how far that still is.

91.title: The team Brazil never beat
91.standfirst: Norway's first World Cup since 1998 has delivered them to the one opponent they have never lost to — and to a Brazil side that has never once solved them.
prose: It reads like the gentlest of asymmetries: five World Cup titles against none, twenty-three appearances against four, an Ancelotti side that topped its group against a team France took apart a fortnight ago. But the fixture carries one inconvenient line of history. Brazil have played Norway four times — in 1988, 1997, 1998 and 2006 — and have never won: two draws, two defeats. Norway are among the very few nations anywhere to have faced Brazil and never lost to them, and on Sunday evening at MetLife that record finally meets knockout football.

The ledger is mostly Oslo friendlies — 1-1 in 1988, a 4-2 Norwegian win in 1997, 1-1 again in 2006 — but the meeting that matters was Marseille, June 1998. Bebeto put the holders ahead with twelve minutes left; Tore André Flo equalised almost immediately, and Kjetil Rekdal's late penalty completed the turnaround. Norway reached the knockout rounds for the first time, and Morocco, 3-0 winners over Scotland that same night, were the side squeezed out. This summer has quietly reassembled the cast: Brazil's group contained both Morocco and Scotland, and Morocco again took points off Brazil — a 1-1 draw at this same stadium in Brazil's opening match. Norway now complete the reunion.

Carlo Ancelotti's first tournament in charge has been steady rather than imperious. After the Morocco draw, Brazil put three past Haiti in Philadelphia and three past Scotland in Miami without conceding, then edged Japan 2-1 in Houston. Vinícius Júnior has four of their nine goals and Matheus Cunha three, with Casemiro and Gabriel Martinelli supplying the others.

Norway's first World Cup in twenty-eight years began at pace: four past Iraq in Boston, then a 3-2 win over Senegal on this ground, before losing 4-1 to France. In Dallas on Tuesday, Erling Haaland's 86th-minute goal saw off Côte d'Ivoire 2-1 and gave Norway the first knockout-round win in their history. Both of their previous last-16 visits, in 1938 and 1998, ended in defeat to Italy; this one, at only their fourth World Cup, already matches the furthest they have ever been.

The football turns on a plain question. Haaland has five of Norway's ten goals — braces against Iraq and Senegal, then the winner in Dallas — and he arrived at this tournament with 55 international goals in 50 caps. Brazil spent the build-up denying that any dedicated anti-Haaland plan exists, a denial that commits them to nothing. Around him, Ståle Solbakken's side have shared the rest: Antonio Nusa, Thelo Aasgaard and the defenders Leo Østigård and Marcus Holmgren Pedersen have all scored. Brazil's threat has been broader and quicker, but Japan showed in Houston that this defence can be reached, and Norway will not need many chances.

For Norway, a quarter-final would be the deepest run in their history. For Brazil, chasing a first title since 2002, the evening carries a subtler discomfort: a knockout tie obliges this fixture, at last, to produce a winner — though a shoot-out, it should be said, could send Brazil through and still leave the old record technically untouched.
threads: Norway are unbeaten in four meetings with Brazil: wins in Oslo 1997 and Marseille 1998, draws in 1988 and 2006.
Haaland has five of Norway's ten tournament goals; he arrived at the World Cup with 55 in 50 for his country.
Brazil, Morocco and Scotland — three-quarters of 1998's Group A — were drawn together again this summer; Norway complete the set tonight.
Norway's only previous last-16 trips, 1938 and 1998, both ended against Italy.
91.meaning: For once, the five-time champions are the ones with something to disprove.

92.title: Back to the Azteca
92.standfirst: Mexico have gone four matches without conceding; England have not played a competitive match at the Azteca since the summer of the Hand of God. The co-hosts meet the tournament's most dependable finisher on the most storied ground the World Cup has.
prose: The Estadio Azteca has staged two World Cup finals and a fair share of the tournament's permanent images, and on Sunday evening it hosts a round of 16 tie that reads like an argument between its own eras. Mexico, co-hosts, arrive unbeaten, with four clean sheets from four matches. England arrive having not played a competitive fixture on this ground since 22 June 1986 — the afternoon Diego Maradona scored twice in four minutes, once with his hand and once with a goal later voted the World Cup's greatest. Nothing about the pairing is neutral.

As a fixture it is thin; as a setting it is anything but. England and Mexico have met nine times, England winning six, and only once at a World Cup — the 1966 group stage at Wembley, won 2-0 through Bobby Charlton and Roger Hunt on the way to England's only title. Mexico took the first meeting, in 1959; two years later England won 8-0 at Wembley, Charlton scoring three. The sides have not met at all since a friendly in 2010. The Azteca itself carries the deeper history. England never played here in 1970 — their group in Guadalajara, their quarter-final in León — but did twice in June 1986, beating Paraguay 3-0 in the round of 16 before Argentina, four days later, ended everything.

Mexico's road to this tie has been the cleanest in the tournament. They opened on this ground with a 2-0 win over South Africa, beat South Korea 1-0 in Guadalajara, then returned to the Azteca to take Czechia apart 3-0 and put out Ecuador 2-0 in the last 32: eight scored, none conceded. Javier Aguirre, in his third spell in charge, has brought Mexico to this stage twice before, in 2002 and 2010, and no further. England's route through the United States was less tidy — 4-2 against Croatia in Dallas, a flat goalless draw with Ghana in Boston, 2-0 against Panama, then a narrow 2-1 win over DR Congo in Atlanta.

The matchup itself is unusually clear: the tournament's tightest defence against its most dependable finisher. Harry Kane has five of England's eight goals, with Jude Bellingham adding two and Marcus Rashford one; nobody else has scored. Mexico's eight have come from five players — Julián Quiñones with three, Raúl Jiménez two, single goals from Luis Romo, Mateo Chávez and Álvaro Fidalgo — a spread that suits a side built from the back. Thomas Tuchel's lingering problem is at right-back, where Reece James remains doubtful, though Jarell Quansah has been passed fit. And there is the ground itself, 2,240 metres up: a thin-air question England have not had to answer in forty years.

The stakes sit unevenly. Both of Mexico's World Cup knockout wins in nearly a century of trying have come at the Azteca — Bulgaria in 1986, Ecuador this week — and victory on Sunday would mean a first quarter-final since 1986, a third in all, every one of them reached at home. England's reward would be quieter but just as real: a place in the last eight, and a new memory from the ground that holds their most replayed defeat.
threads: The Azteca is the only stadium to have staged two World Cup finals — 1970 and 1986 — and this summer it became the first to host three tournaments.
The only previous World Cup meeting: England 2-0 Mexico in the 1966 group at Wembley, Charlton and Hunt scoring, en route to England's title.
Both of Mexico's World Cup knockout victories have come at the Azteca: Bulgaria in 1986 and Ecuador in this tournament's last 32.
Kane has five of England's eight goals; Mexico's eight are spread across five scorers, with none conceded in four matches.
92.meaning: The Azteca keeps the best of Mexico's World Cup past and the worst of England's; on Sunday it adds to one of the collections.

93.title: Iberia in Texas
93.standfirst: Portugal and Spain share a peninsula and a long habit of avoiding each other when it matters most. Monday in Dallas is only their second World Cup knockout meeting.
prose: The first was Cape Town in 2010: David Villa turned in the only goal, and Spain went on to win the tournament. Sixteen years later the second arrives at AT&T Stadium, about as far from the peninsula as the fixture could reasonably be staged. For Spain, the reward for a month without conceding is the neighbour they can never quite shake. For Portugal, it is the examination their tournament has been building towards.

The rivalry lives mostly in club football, but the tournament meetings have a habit of mattering. At Euro 2004, Nuno Gomes's goal helped put the Spanish out at the group stage. At Euro 2012, Spain needed a semi-final shootout, Cesc Fàbregas converting the decisive kick. In Sochi in 2018 the sides shared six goals, Cristiano Ronaldo completing his hat-trick — at 33, the oldest man to score one at a World Cup — with an 88th-minute free kick. And in June 2025 they contested the Nations League final in Munich: 2-2 after extra time, Portugal taking the shootout when Diogo Costa saved from Álvaro Morata. The recent ledger is more even than the reputations.

Spain's month has been nearly silent. A goalless opening against Cabo Verde in Atlanta read as a blemish at the time; it now stands as the only match they have failed to win, and it came against the smallest nation ever to reach the knockout rounds. Since then, Saudi Arabia were beaten 4-0, Uruguay 1-0, Austria 3-0. Eight scored, none conceded. Mikel Oyarzabal — a scorer in that Munich final — has four of the goals; Lamine Yamal, who carries most of the country's expectation, Álex Baena and Pedro Porro have one apiece.

Portugal's route has been rougher. Held by DR Congo in Houston, emphatic against Uzbekistan, goalless against Colombia, they finished second in their group and were sent to Toronto, where the round-of-32 tie with Croatia distilled their tournament: behind to Ivan Perišić, level through Ronaldo's penalty, ahead in the fourth minute of stoppage time when Gonçalo Ramos headed in Rafael Leão's cross. Croatia believed they had equalised even later; the review found an offside in the build-up. Portugal advanced on conviction rather than control.

There is a quiet irony in the dugouts: Portugal are picked by Roberto Martínez, a Spaniard from Balaguer who beat his own country in that Munich final, while Luis de la Fuente's Spain have yet to concede to anyone. Ronaldo, 41 now and at a sixth World Cup, has three of Portugal's goals; Leão, Ramos, João Neves and Nuno Mendes have added one each. The stakes sit unevenly. Spain, champions in 2010, are pursuing a second title and look constructed for it. Portugal's best remains third place in 1966; they have never played a World Cup final. The border is drawn again on Monday, this time across a Texas afternoon.
threads: Spain have scored eight and conceded none; the 0-0 with Cabo Verde is the only game they have not won
Spain won the sides' only previous World Cup knockout tie 1-0 in Cape Town in 2010, David Villa scoring
Portugal took the June 2025 Nations League final in Munich 5-3 on penalties after a 2-2 draw; Nuno Mendes and Oyarzabal scored that night and have scored here too
Ronaldo's 88th-minute free kick in the 3-3 at Sochi in 2018 made him, at 33, the oldest scorer of a World Cup hat-trick
93.meaning: One peninsula, one place in the last eight.

94.title: As old as the tournament
94.standfirst: The United States and Belgium have met at World Cups twice — on the tournament's first day in 1930, and on Tim Howard's long night in Salvador in 2014. Monday at Lumen Field decides who gets a quarter-final.
prose: On Monday evening in Seattle, the United States play the kind of match a home World Cup exists for. Mauricio Pochettino's side have reached the last sixteen of a tournament they are hosting, and their reward is Belgium — at a fifteenth World Cup, third in 2018, and rebuilt by Rudi García around the survivors of the golden generation. For one of these teams the summer continues. For the other, the reckoning starts on Tuesday morning.

The fixture is as old as the tournament itself. When these countries first met, on 13 July 1930 at the Parque Central in Montevideo, it was the opening day of the first World Cup; the Americans won 3-0, reached the semi-finals, and the third place credited to that team is still their best finish. The second meeting needs less introduction. Salvador, 2014, this same round: Kevin De Bruyne and Romelu Lukaku scored in extra time, Julian Green pulled one back, Belgium won 2-1, and Tim Howard made sixteen saves — the most recorded in a World Cup match since FIFA first kept the statistic in 1966, a record that still stood when this tournament kicked off.

The hosts arrived here in a straight line with one kink in it. They put four past Paraguay in Los Angeles, beat Australia 2-0 in Seattle, then lost 3-2 to Türkiye back in Los Angeles — their only defeat — before a 2-0 win over Bosnia & Herzegovina in the Bay Area in the last 32. Belgium's route was the reverse shape: level with Egypt in Seattle and goalless against Iran in Los Angeles, then five against New Zealand in Vancouver and a 3-2 win over Senegal in the knockout opener. The ledgers are nearly identical — ten scored and four conceded for the United States, nine and four for Belgium.

The goals describe how each side works. Folarin Balogun has three of the American ten, but six different players have scored, Giovanni Reyna and Malik Tillman among them; the burden is spread. Belgium's nine are shared almost evenly — Leandro Trossard, Youri Tielemans and Lukaku have two apiece, and De Bruyne, a scorer in Salvador twelve years ago, has one here too. There is also the matter of the ground. This will be Belgium's third match of the tournament at Lumen Field; the United States have played there once, and won.

The stakes sit differently on each side. The Americans have staged a World Cup before, and it ended at exactly this stage — Brazil, 1-0, at Stanford on 4 July 1994. Salvador closed a tournament at this stage too. A quarter-final would carry a home World Cup further than one has ever taken them. For Belgium, it would be evidence that what came after the golden generation is a team in its own right rather than an afterglow. Two previous meetings, one win each, ninety-six years apart; the third settles more than a bracket position.
threads: The sides have split their two World Cup meetings: USA 3-0 in Montevideo on the opening day in 1930, Belgium 2-1 after extra time in Salvador in 2014.
Tim Howard's 16 saves against Belgium in 2014 entered this tournament as the most recorded in a World Cup match since FIFA began counting the statistic in 1966.
Belgium play their third match of this tournament at Lumen Field, after 1-1 with Egypt and 3-2 over Senegal; the USA beat Australia 2-0 there in the group.
De Bruyne and Lukaku, Belgium's extra-time scorers in 2014, have both scored again at this World Cup.
94.meaning: Ninety-six years after the first meeting, each side is playing to prove its best World Cup is not already behind it.

95.title: Two eras cross in Atlanta
95.standfirst: Argentina and Egypt have met twice in ninety-eight years, never at a World Cup. In Atlanta, the holders' title defence runs into the first Egypt side ever to win World Cup matches — and Messi, at last, shares a pitch with Salah.
prose: The round of 16 mostly trades in familiar arguments. This tie has none to trade. Argentina and Egypt have never met at a World Cup, and Tuesday's midday kick-off at Mercedes-Benz Stadium is only their third senior meeting in ninety-eight years. What the fixture offers instead is a crossing the game never got around to arranging: Lionel Messi, 39 and seven goals into Argentina's title defence, against Mohamed Salah, 34 and captain of the first Egypt side ever to win a World Cup match.

The prior file is thin and one-sided. In the semi-final of the 1928 Olympic tournament in Amsterdam, Argentina beat Egypt 6-0, Domingo Tarasconi scoring three, before losing the final to Uruguay. The sides did not meet again for eighty years, until a friendly in March 2008 that Argentina won 2-0; Messi was absent. Salah was fifteen at the time. Neither man has ever faced the other's country, and the first time arrives with a quarter-final attached.

Argentina's route was serene until it abruptly wasn't. Algeria were dispatched 3-0 in Kansas City, Messi helping himself to a hat-trick; Austria and Jordan followed in Dallas, Messi scoring in both, the last of them ten minutes from time. Then Cabo Verde, the smallest nation ever to reach a World Cup knockout round, dragged the champions into extra time in Miami. Messi opened after 29 minutes, Argentina were twice pegged back — Cabral levelled deep in extra time — and the 3-2 win was not safe until the final minutes. Seven of Argentina's eleven goals this tournament are Messi's.

Egypt's tournament belongs to a different order of history. They arrived having never won in three previous World Cups — one match in 1934, three in 1990, three in 2018 — and now have two wins in a fortnight. The 3-1 over New Zealand in Vancouver, sandwiched between 1-1 draws with Belgium and Iran in Seattle, was the country's first World Cup victory, ninety-two years after their debut. In Dallas, Emam Ashour's thirteenth-minute goal against Australia was cancelled out by Mohamed Hany's own goal, his second of the tournament, and Egypt won the shoot-out 4-2 without missing a kick, Salah among the scorers and Hossam Abdelmaguid converting the winner. It was their first knockout tie since the 1934 debut — a 4-2 defeat to Hungary in Naples under the old straight-knockout format — and their first knockout win ever.

A thread in the Egypt camp predates Salah. Hossam Hassan, the coach, scored the 1989 qualifying goal against Algeria that ended a fifty-six-year absence, then led the line at Italia 90, where Egypt drew twice and went out to a single England goal. His team defend in that image: three 1-1 draws in four games, chances rationed, the big moments taken. Argentina pose the opposite problem, their goals spread through Lo Celso, Lautaro Martínez and Lisandro Martínez around the seven from Messi. For Scaloni's side, a quarter-final is simply the next obligation of a defence. For Egypt, everything past Tuesday is unmapped.
threads: The only previous meetings: a 6-0 Olympic semi-final in Amsterdam in 1928 and a 2-0 friendly in 2008 that Messi missed.
Messi has seven of Argentina's eleven goals this tournament, starting with a hat-trick against Algeria.
Egypt's 3-1 over New Zealand was their first win in four World Cup appearances stretching back to 1934.
Hossam Hassan scored the 1989 qualifier that took Egypt to Italia 90, played there, and now coaches them past it.
95.meaning: Not a rivalry but an intersection — two careers that defined their countries, crossing exactly once, this late and this deep in.

96.title: The quiet tie of the eight
96.standfirst: Switzerland and Colombia meet at BC Place with the round's lowest billing and perhaps its most even question: whether a side that has conceded once in a month can be moved.
prose: Eight ties make up this round, and this is the one the previews skim. No holders, no hosts, no bad blood — Switzerland and Colombia at BC Place on Tuesday afternoon, two unbeaten sides with the same historical ceiling. Each has reached a quarter-final and gone no further: Switzerland in 1934, 1938 and 1954, Colombia in 2014. The prize here is not a famous scalp. It is a run at their own high-water mark.

They have met at a World Cup exactly once, and the memory is a strange one. Stanford, June 1994: Hernán Gaviria headed Colombia in front just before half-time, Harold Lozano added a second in the final minute, and a gifted side that had malfunctioned for two matches produced its best football too late. Colombia won 2-0 and still went home on three points; Switzerland lost and went through to the last 16. It remains that rare fixture in which defeat was the better evening. Tuesday is their first meeting in a knockout round.

Switzerland's route has settled into a routine. After a flat 1-1 with Qatar they beat Bosnia and Herzegovina 4-1, took the group from Canada with a 2-1 win in Vancouver — the result that denied the co-hosts a home last-32 tie — then put out Algeria 2-0 at the same ground. This is their third consecutive match at BC Place; no visiting side left in the draw has a better claim to feeling at home. Colombia's route has been longer and quieter: 3-1 over Uzbekistan in Mexico City, then the shutters came down — 1-0 against DR Congo, 0-0 with Portugal in Miami, 1-0 over Ghana in Kansas City through Jhon Arias's early goal. One goal conceded in four matches, and three straight clean sheets for the first time in their World Cup history.

The football promises a fair contest between a set defence and a spread attack, though the roles are less fixed than they look. Néstor Lorenzo's Colombia commit their full-backs, and the scoring chart shows it: Daniel Muñoz leads with two, while James Rodríguez still runs the supply. Murat Yakin's Switzerland have shared nine goals among five scorers, led by Johan Manzambi's three. Manzambi is the Swiss find of the summer: a 20-year-old Freiburg midfielder, Geneva-born, who scored twice in sixteen minutes against Bosnia — at 20 years and 247 days the youngest Swiss to score twice in a World Cup match — then scored again against Canada. Breel Embolo and Ruben Vargas carry two each, with Granit Xhaka setting the tempo behind them.

The stakes, stated plainly: the winner takes a quarter-final place Colombia have held once and Switzerland have not touched since they hosted in 1954 — eight years before Colombia had played a World Cup at all. Since 1994 the Swiss have reached the last 16 five times and lost every one. Neither country would call this era a failure, yet each keeps meeting the same wall. The quietest tie of the eight has the most patient queue behind it.
threads: Colombia's only goal conceded came in their opener; three consecutive clean sheets since is a first for them at a World Cup.
Manzambi's brace against Bosnia, at 20 years and 247 days, made him the youngest Swiss to score twice in a World Cup match.
Switzerland play a third straight match at BC Place; Colombia arrive via Mexico City, Guadalajara, Miami and Kansas City.
The sides' only World Cup meeting, Stanford 1994: Colombia won 2-0 and were eliminated that night, while beaten Switzerland advanced.
96.meaning: Two countries with the same old ceiling, and one quiet afternoon to test it.

97.title: The Doha rematch
97.standfirst: Nearly four years after Al Khor, the last World Cup's semi-finalists meet again — France having conceded nothing in the knockouts, Morocco having survived a shootout to get here.
prose: France arrive at this quarter-final the way they have arrived at most of them under Didier Deschamps: without fuss, and without conceding. They beat Sweden 3-0 in the round of 32 and Paraguay 1-0 in the round of 16, and no side has yet found a way through them in the knockout rounds. It is the familiar shape of a Deschamps tournament, patience where it is needed and enough at the other end, in what he has said will be his last competition in charge.

Morocco have taken the harder road. Held 1-1 by the Netherlands in the round of 32, they went to penalties and won the shootout 3-2. The round of 16 was more straightforward — 3-0 against the co-hosts Canada, Azzedine Ounahi scoring twice — and it carried Walid Regragui's side into a second consecutive World Cup quarter-final, the stage that four years ago became something more.

For this is a rematch, and both sides know exactly which one. In December 2022 they met in the semi-final at Al Bayt, in Al Khor, and France won 2-0: Théo Hernández volleying in inside five minutes, Randal Kolo Muani turning in a second late on, moments after coming off the bench. France went to the final; Morocco went to the third-place match, the first African and first Arab nation to reach a World Cup semi-final. That night is the memory Morocco carry into this one.

The routes here read almost as inversions of each other. France have controlled their matches and kept clean sheets; Morocco have ridden the fine margins — a 90th-minute equaliser, a shootout, a goalkeeper — and come through them intact. One side has looked comfortable and one has looked resilient, and the quarter-final asks which of those holds up when the other is across the halfway line.

What is different from Doha is the surrounding shape of things. That semi-final was the furthest any African nation had ever gone at a World Cup; this time they are among the last eight as a matter of expectation rather than surprise, and they have done it the hard way twice already. France, for their part, have changed little — the same manager, the same refusal to concede — and are back at the stage they have reached in every tournament Deschamps has overseen.

So the tie is a settling of a specific account, or an attempt at one. France beat Morocco when it mattered most last time and have given nothing away since arriving in North America. Morocco lost that night and have spent this tournament proving they can survive the situations that end other teams. The quarter-final puts the two versions of that history in the same fixture again, with the semi-final on the other side of it.
threads: The sides last met in the 2022 World Cup semi-final at Al Bayt Stadium, Al Khor, where France won 2-0 through Théo Hernández and Randal Kolo Muani.
Morocco were the first African and first Arab nation to reach a World Cup semi-final, in 2022.
France have not conceded in the knockout rounds this tournament: 3-0 against Sweden, 1-0 against Paraguay.
Morocco reached this stage via a 3-2 shootout win over the Netherlands after a 1-1 draw, then a 3-0 win over Canada.
Both managers remain from Doha: Didier Deschamps for France, Walid Regragui for Morocco.
97.meaning: The same two teams, the same stage as Doha — one arriving unbreached, the other carrying what happened there.

98.title: The debt of Puebla
98.standfirst: Forty years after Belgium ended a Spanish World Cup on penalties in Puebla, the two meet again at the same stage — one side winning narrow, the other winning wide.
prose: The last time these teams met at a World Cup quarter-final, the tie would not resolve itself. Puebla, June 1986: Jan Ceulemans put Belgium ahead after half an hour, Señor equalised with five minutes left, and 1-1 held through extra time. In the shoot-out Belgium scored all five and won 5-4. Spain went home; Belgium went on to the semi-finals, the deepest run in their history. Forty years on, the fixture returns to precisely the round where it last mattered.

The record between them is short and evenly split. Four years after Puebla, in Verona at Italia '90, Spain answered, winning 2-1 — a result that sent Spain through as group winners, with Belgium behind them. Two World Cup meetings, then, one apiece, the older of them still owed. Belgium have the shoot-out; Spain have the only ninety-minute win.

The routes here could hardly be more different in temperament. Spain have won by the narrowest agreed margins the knockouts allow — well, not quite: they opened with a 3-0 against Austria in the round of 32, then squeezed past Portugal 1-0 in the round of 16, an Iberian derby settled by a single goal. Luis de la Fuente's side, European champions two summers ago, have arrived at the last eight having learned to defend a lead rather than extend one.

Belgium have taken the opposite path. Rudi Garcia, in charge only since the start of 2025, has a team that keeps scoring and keeps conceding: 3-2 past Senegal in the round of 32, then 4-1 against the United States in the round of 16. Seven goals in two knockout matches, three let in — a side that treats every tie as an exchange rather than a siege, and has so far come out ahead of the exchange each time.

So the quarter-final sets a plain contradiction. Spain want the game narrow, low, decided by the one moment they can control; Belgium want it open, and trust their own weight of goals to settle it. Whichever team imposes its tempo tends to impose the result — and the other history hangs over it too, quietly, because Spain have lost three of their four World Cup shoot-outs, and one of those three was here, against these opponents, at this stage.

A semi-final place is the prize, and for both it would carry a particular weight: for Belgium, a return to the last four they reached in 1986 and 2018; for Spain, a first World Cup semi-final since they won the whole thing in 2010. The tie that closed in Puebla with a Belgian five from five reopens with nothing yet decided — and, this time, no shoot-out owed until the football has been played.
threads: 1986 quarter-final, Puebla: 1-1 after extra time, Belgium won the shoot-out 5-4, scoring all five of their kicks.
1990 group stage, Verona: Spain 2-1 Belgium, which sent Spain through as group winners.
Spain's knockout run has been controlled — 3-0 v Austria, then 1-0 v Portugal in an Iberian derby.
Belgium have scored seven and conceded three across two knockout ties — 3-2 v Senegal, 4-1 v USA.
Spain have lost three of their four World Cup penalty shoot-outs; the 1986 defeat to Belgium was one of them.
98.meaning: A tie that once needed penalties to separate them returns with a semi-final at stake and the old debt still standing.

99.title: The outsiders and the old habit
99.standfirst: Norway, in their first World Cup quarter-final and fresh from removing Brazil, meet an England side that has spent this tournament finding ways to win the close ones — two nations who have never once met at a World Cup.
prose: It is, on paper, the meeting the draw was least likely to produce. Norway had reached the knockout rounds only twice before this summer, and never gone beyond them; England have been to the last eight and further often enough that the stages themselves carry a weight of memory. Yet both arrive by the same route — a sequence of tight matches decided late — and both arrive without any shared World Cup history at all. In more than a century of the tournament, Norway and England have never been drawn together on this stage. Whatever the tie becomes, it starts from nothing.

The two nations are not strangers away from the finals. They first played in 1937, and met on and off through the friendlies of the following decades; the most recent meeting was a 1-0 England win at Wembley in 2014, Wayne Rooney converting a penalty. But a World Cup match is new ground for both, and the setting reframes the familiarity. England have the longer record and the heavier expectation. Norway have the momentum of a side that has already done the thing nobody asked of them.

Norway's road here has been the story of the round. Ståle Solbakken's team came through the group at pace, then edged Côte d'Ivoire 2-1 in Dallas, Erling Haaland's late goal delivering the first knockout-round win in the country's history. In the last 16 they went further still, beating Brazil 2-1 — the upset of the round, and the result that turned a good tournament into a historic one. Norway have reached the World Cup only four times, in 1938, 1994, 1998 and this summer; both of their previous knockout appearances ended against Italy. A quarter-final is territory the country has never occupied.

England's progress has been quieter and more familiar in shape: the tidy group work of a well-drilled side, then two knockout ties settled by a single goal. They saw off DR Congo 2-1 in the last 32 and came through a more open evening against Mexico, winning 3-2 in the round of 16. Thomas Tuchel's team have not been imperious, but they have been hard to put away, and the pattern of narrow wins has carried them to the last eight without the drama their tournaments sometimes invite.

The contrast the tie offers is less about styles than about weather. England's World Cup past is bound up with the penalty shoot-out — four of them, in 1990, 1998, 2006 and 2018, and only the last, against Colombia, won. The 2006 defeat, to Portugal, came at this very stage. None of that decides anything in advance, but it hangs over every England knockout tie that stays level, and Norway are exactly the kind of opponent — organised, unhurried, carrying a forward who needs one opening — who might keep one level. Haaland has been the difference already; whether he is given the room to be it again is the question the match is built around.

For Norway, the meaning is simple arithmetic: win, and they equal nothing in their own history because there is nothing to equal — they would be somewhere the country has never been. For England, the stakes are the usual ones, familiar to the point of discomfort: a semi-final within reach, and an old habit waiting to be either broken or repeated. The outsiders removed the favourites once this month. They will not mind being cast that way again.
threads: Norway and England have never met at a World Cup finals; away from the tournament they have played since 1937, most recently a 1-0 England win at Wembley in 2014
This is Norway's first World Cup quarter-final; their only previous knockout trips, in 1938 and 1998, both ended against Italy
Norway beat Côte d'Ivoire 2-1 and then Brazil 2-1 to reach the last eight; England came through 2-1 against DR Congo and 3-2 against Mexico
England have contested four World Cup penalty shoot-outs — 1990, 1998, 2006 and 2018 — and won only the last, against Colombia; the 2006 defeat, to Portugal, came in the quarter-final
Haaland's goal against Côte d'Ivoire was the first knockout-round win in Norway's World Cup history
99.meaning: One side has never been this far; the other has been here often enough to know exactly what can go wrong.

100.title: The narrow way through
100.standfirst: The holders arrive at the last eight having twice been taken to the final minutes; Switzerland arrive having learned to win without scoring.
prose: Argentina have not had it easy, and it shows. The defending champions saw off Cabo Verde 3-2 in the round of 32, then Egypt by the same 3-2 in the round of 16, two matches carried to the wire and settled by the odd goal. For a side that lifted the trophy last time, the route has been less a procession than a series of held breaths.

Switzerland have travelled by a quieter road, and a colder one. They dealt with Algeria 2-0 in the round of 32, controlled and unhurried, then met Colombia in the round of 16 and gave nothing away across 120 goalless minutes before winning the shootout 4-3. It is the mark of a team that has decided a clean sheet is a plan rather than a hope.

So the tie sets two temperaments against each other. Argentina have scored freely and conceded more than they would like; Switzerland have scored sparingly and conceded almost nothing. One side has been dragged into open, breathless games and found a way through each time. The other has narrowed the pitch, slowed the tempo, and trusted the margins to hold.

The history belongs entirely to Argentina, and part of it belongs to this stage. The countries met in the 1966 group phase, Argentina winning 2-0 in a tournament Switzerland left without a point. They met again at the 2014 World Cup, in the round of 16, where the game stayed level until Angel Di Maria struck in extra time to settle it 1-0. Twice at a World Cup, twice Argentina have come out the right side.

That 2014 evening is the one that lingers. Switzerland held the world's more celebrated side for almost two hours and were minutes from a shootout before Lionel Messi slipped the pass that Di Maria finished. It is the exact shape of game Switzerland have built themselves to survive this summer, and the exact margin on which it turned against them.

What faces them now is a champion side that keeps finding the extra goal when the match demands it, and a Swiss side that keeps refusing to concede the first. Both have already spent longer on the pitch than they intended. Neither looks likely to make the eighth of these matches a comfortable one.
threads: Argentina reached the last eight the hard way: 3-2 over Cabo Verde in the round of 32, then 3-2 over Egypt in the round of 16, both settled by a single goal.
Switzerland have not conceded in the knockouts, beating Algeria 2-0 before a goalless draw with Colombia that they won 4-3 on penalties.
The countries have met twice at a World Cup, both won by Argentina: 2-0 in the 1966 group stage and 1-0 in the 2014 round of 16.
The 2014 tie was scoreless until the second period of extra time, when Angel Di Maria scored from a Lionel Messi pass with the shootout approaching.
Argentina come into the quarter-final as the defending champions.
100.meaning: A settled champion that has learned to win late meets a side built to make sure the game is still there to be won late.

stars.name: Lionel MESSI
stars.line: 39 · FW · Inter Miami CF · 8 goals — hat-trick v Algeria, 2 v Austria, 1 v Jordan, opener v Cabo Verde; R16 v Egypt: the 83' equaliser in the 3-2 comeback
stars.why: The record is settled — twenty-one World Cup goals, more than anyone — and in the round of 16 the tournament asked what it was for. Argentina trailed Egypt 2-0 with eleven minutes left; Messi answered with the 83rd-minute equaliser that made the comeback possible before Enzo Fernández won it in stoppage time. At 39, at his sixth World Cup, the holders still turn to him when a match is slipping. It is habit now, not sentiment.

stars.name: Enzo FERNANDEZ
stars.tag: The header that saved the holders
stars.line: 25 · MF · Chelsea FC · his stoppage-time header beat Egypt 3-2 after Argentina had trailed 2-0 in the 79th minute · R32 3-2 aet v Cabo Verde
stars.why: Argentina's defence of the title has twice been taken to the edge, and in Atlanta it went past it: two goals down to Egypt with eleven minutes to play, one round after Cabo Verde had held them into extra time. Cristian Romero's header offered a lifeline, Messi levelled, and Fernández headed the winner in the second minute of added time to complete one of the great World Cup recoveries. The champions stayed on course for a successive title having, twice now, looked like leaving early.

stars.name: Kylian MBAPPE
stars.line: 27 · FW · Real Madrid · 7 goals — braces v Senegal, Iraq and Sweden, then the 70' penalty that beat Paraguay 1-0 · a fourth straight quarter-final for France
stars.why: France have been the tournament's most fluent attacking side, and he is its sharpest edge: braces against Senegal, Iraq and Sweden, then the single clean moment Philadelphia's 38-degree heat allowed — the 70th-minute penalty that took France past Paraguay into a fourth consecutive quarter-final. It was his 19th World Cup goal, at 27, one behind Messi's all-time twenty; the two share this tournament's lead on seven. Morocco are next, a rematch of the 2022 semi-final. He no longer has to carry France; he finishes what a very good side builds.

stars.name: Yassine BOUNOU
stars.line: 35 · GK · Al Hilal · 90 caps before the tournament · Morocco: 1-1 Brazil, R32 1-1 v Netherlands (3-2 pens), R16 3-0 v Canada
stars.why: The pattern is established. In 2022 he kept Spain scoreless for 120 minutes and saved two kicks in the shoot-out; this time the Netherlands were sent home from one, and against co-hosts Canada he kept a clean sheet as Morocco pulled clear. Two World Cups running, a European side has left a shoot-out with Bounou at the centre of it. Morocco reach a second successive quarter-final unbeaten at this tournament. Calm is a skill; his has aged well.

stars.name: Azzedine OUNAHI
stars.tag: The brace that beat the co-hosts
stars.line: 26 · MF · Girona FC · 2 goals — 50' and 82' in the 3-0 R16 win over Canada · Morocco unbeaten in five, the Netherlands beaten 3-2 on penalties
stars.why: Four years ago he was the unknown who left Spain's coach asking, mid-tournament, where he had come from. In Houston he was the certainty: a goal either side of the hour, on 50 and 82 minutes, before Soufiane Rahimi added a third. Morocco have gone through the tournament unbeaten — Brazil held, the Netherlands outlasted on penalties — and conceded once in the knockout rounds. France come next, who beat them in the 2022 semi-final; a debt has been carried four years to be settled.

stars.name: Mikel OYARZABAL
stars.line: 29 · FW · Real Sociedad · 2 goals in the 3-0 R32 win over Austria (36' and 89') · Spain: R16 1-0 v Portugal
stars.why: The man who scored the goal that won Spain the last European Championship has been their most reliable finish here, twice beating Austria to end a fifteen-year wait for a World Cup knockout win. He might have had the Portugal tie too, spurning a clear chance late before Mikel Merino settled it. Spain have reached the quarter-finals without conceding in the knockout rounds, their two Iberian and Alpine tests met without alarm. Belgium, and their long unbeaten run, are what stands next.

stars.name: Mikel MERINO
stars.tag: The substitute who ended Ronaldo's World Cups
stars.line: 30 · MF · Arsenal FC · came off the bench to score the injury-time winner in Spain's 1-0 R16 defeat of Portugal
stars.why: A low, cagey Iberian derby was heading for extra time when Merino, on as a substitute, followed in his own quick free-kick and finished past Diogo Costa in the first minute of added time. The goal put Spain into the last eight and closed Cristiano Ronaldo's World Cup career, the 41-year-old a passenger for much of a night his side played too carefully. Spain have not conceded in the knockouts; the quiet man from the bench decided the round that promised the most noise.

stars.name: Charles DE KETELAERE
stars.line: 25 · FW · Atalanta BC · scored twice (9', 33') in Belgium's 4-1 R16 win over the United States · R32 3-2 aet v Senegal
stars.why: Belgium spent the round of 32 clinging on, beating Senegal only through a stoppage-time equaliser and a contested extra-time penalty. Against the co-hosts they were something else: De Ketelaere scored inside nine minutes, added a second before the half, exposing the United States' defence in a 4-1 win. It stretched Belgium's unbeaten run to eighteen matches and carried a side that had looked vulnerable into a quarter-final with Spain. The talent long spoken of arrived on the night it was most needed.

stars.name: Erling HAALAND
stars.tag: The two goals that removed Brazil
stars.line: 25 · FW · Manchester City · 7 goals — 2 v Iraq, 2 v Senegal, 86' winner v Côte d'Ivoire (R32), then 79' and 90' to beat Brazil 2-1 (R16)
stars.why: Norway's first World Cup in 28 years, Haaland's first at all, and in the round of 16 it produced the upset of the tournament: two goals in the final eleven minutes against Brazil, after Ørjan Nyland had saved Bruno Guimarães' early penalty. The five-time winners went out; Norway reached a quarter-final for the first time in their history. He arrived with 55 goals in 50 internationals and the tournament has not slowed the rate. Norway have still never lost to Brazil, and now they have knocked them out.

stars.name: Harry KANE
stars.tag: Past Pelé on World Cup goals
stars.line: 32 · FW · FC Bayern München · 6 goals — 2 v Croatia, 1 v Panama, 2 v DR Congo (R32), penalty v Mexico (R16)
stars.why: Kane's tournament has been quietly complete. His brace against DR Congo took him past Pelé's World Cup total; his 60th-minute penalty against Mexico kept England ahead in a 3-2 win they finished with ten men after Jarell Quansah's red card. At 32 he keeps arriving where matches are decided, the reliable half of an England attack that has found a second scorer beside him. Norway, and Erling Haaland, are the quarter-final; two of the tournament's surest finishers on the same field.

stars.name: Jude BELLINGHAM
stars.line: 23 · MF · Real Madrid · 4 goals — 1 v Croatia, 1 v Panama, then two v Mexico (36', 38') in the 3-2 R16 win
stars.why: England's second scorer has grown into the tournament. Two goals in two minutes against Mexico put England in control before Jarell Quansah's red card early in the second half left them to defend a lead a man short; they held, with Kane's penalty the margin, and reached the last eight. At 23 Bellingham now carries a share of England's goals as well as its midfield, four of them across the run. The brace came in the round of 16, under the most pressure the tournament has asked of England so far.

stars.name: Gregor KOBEL
stars.tag: The save that sent Switzerland through
stars.line: 28 · GK · Borussia Dortmund · kept out Colombia through 120 goalless minutes, then saved in the shoot-out as Switzerland won 4-3 · R32 2-0 v Algeria
stars.why: Switzerland had not won a World Cup knockout match since 1938. In Vancouver they ended the wait the hard way: a goalless draw with Colombia across two hours, then a shoot-out that Switzerland won 4-3, Kobel's save the difference, to reach a quarter-final for the first time in 72 years. A well-organised side finally found the margin that had eluded it at the last three tournaments, and its goalkeeper supplied it.
